consensus_summary: Egypt primarily and settledly symbolizes bondage/slavery to sin and the oppressive world-system opposed to God, from which He delivers His people, via Exodus typology (with secondary uses as false trust, refuge, or eschatological object).
book_summary: Egypt spiritually denotes Jerusalem—the whore of Babylon that rides the beast, the city that kills the prophets and where the Lord was crucified.
consensus_core_identification: bondage to sin / the world-system (from which God redeems)
book_core_identification: Jerusalem (the city that kills the prophets / whore of Babylon)
boundary_disagreement: Consensus extends Egypt to the general condition of spiritual bondage or any analogous oppressive world-power; book reassigns the spiritual identity exclusively to Jerusalem as the prophetic city.
material_contradiction: Consensus core is an abstract typological condition (bondage/world); book replaces that referent with a concrete city (Jerusalem). The two cannot both be the primary spiritual identification of Egypt in the same sense.
rationale: All blind responses converge on bondage/sin/the world as the dominant, settled Christian symbol grounded in the Exodus. The book explicitly notes that common teaching yet defines Egypt as Jerusalem via Rev 11:8’s ‘great city 	au where also our Lord was crucified’ plus parallel language for Babylon/Jerusalem. Although minority alternatives in the consensus already flag ‘apostate Jerusalem’ as one possible cipher for the Rev 11:8 city, the book elevates that reading into the core meaning of the term itself, thereby substituting a different referent rather than refining the consensus category.
strongest_objection: Rev 11:8 says the great city is spiritually called Egypt (the city is typified by Egypt’s oppression), so Egypt remains the type rather than being identical to Jerusalem; the equation therefore inverts the metaphor and overrides the broader Exodus consensus.
